title: Making Impatience With Results About You First
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles a common leadership misstep: directing frustration about missed deadlines or poor quality at the team, which team members interpret as blame and respond to with defensiveness and reduced motivation rather than urgency. The fix the piece proposes is reframing impatience as a statement about the leader's own responsibility rather than an accusation against others — swapping 'why did you miss the deadline' for 'what can I do to get this finished' or 'what resources do you need.' This flips the emotional register from blame to shared problem-solving while still communicating that the outcome matters, which the piece argues produces more durable urgency than blame-driven pressure.
points: Directing impatience at team members is usually heard as blame, even when leaders don't intend it that way.
Blame-driven pressure produces short-term compliance but longer-term defensiveness and demotivation.
The fix is reframing impatience as being about the leader's own responsibility, not the team's failure.
Practical examples: swapping 'why did you miss the deadline' for 'what can I do to get this finished.'
This reframing keeps urgency about outcomes intact while removing the sting of personal accusation.
quotes: They presume that directing their frustration and intolerance for delays and unrealized expectations toward all those involved will light a fire and increase their urgency and attention to detail.
Team members interpret a leader’s impatience with results as an accusation. They hear the leader blaming them.
What impatient leaders believe will light a fire actually douses the flame.
Leaders who make their impatience about themselves express their frustration with results, not people.
Leaders who direct their impatience at themselves communicate the importance of outcomes without the accusation of blame.
